item.content:encoded:
So far as I am aware, vampires only became associated with the borderlands between Hungary and Romania as a result of Dracula; vampire-like creatures are a pretty universal phenomenon in folklore, but vampires-as-vampires date from the 18th century in Eastern Europe more broadly.

Look, I establish the region in the context of this article's fiction is associated with vampires. If you demand that my vampire fiction is 100% accurate to the historical traditions then I'd have to remove sunlight as a weakness too1, since that only becomes a part of the myth in 1922. I don't care these vampires aren't accurate to folklore traditions: I'm trying to make them consistent with a reader's expectations.

Footnotes
1. This is a bit nuanced but "burning up in sunlight" is 1922 and that's the version of the sunlight weakness I'm using.

item.content:encoded:
I'm going to mostly piggy-back off the latter half of what ARD said here.

+ show block
– hide block

To me it feels like the focus of this article is really on Chaz, rather than the establishment or the food. There's not a lot of time spend developing the place, or the narrator, or his relationship to food (or to being a vampire!) beyond a surface-level. There's a lot of groundwork being laid about the rules of vampires, but they're either things that the reader likely already knows (stay out of the sunlight!) or stuff that is glossed over (hospitality rites). This seems confusing at first, but I think it's supposed to set our expectations for Chaz himself.

The issue then is twofold. One, the reveal that Chaz isn't a vampire falls really flat. In the article we actually spend very little time getting to know Chaz - he doesn't show up till, like, 70% through, and then he's not actually present for the hunt. So the reveal doesn't really land as meaningful because the article doesn't present Chaz as anything other than "chef who is a vampire".

The second issue is that this article is clearly intended to be a part of a greater whole. And in that lens, as ARD points out above, I feel like we actually don't learn anything about Chaz that wasn't already well established - he's cannibal Elon Musk, but for restaurants.

an entire race of people defined by the need to eat.

I think Chaz is the least interesting part about Ambrose, personally. Vampires are frequently defined by hedonism, but what does a hedonist who no longer can experience pleasures of the flesh look like? I would love to see a version of this article that really drills down on the thoughts and perspectives of an immortal vampire who cannot eat, and his relationship to food, time, pleasure, and the experience of being. What would it be like for someone to taste something for the first time in 3 centuries? How does that experience change someone?

item.content:encoded:
Transylvania is an actual place populated by actual humans with some actually pretty interesting history.

Here, as elsewhere, it is just "le epic vampire country." If this was "Ambrose - Dayton, Ohio, But There Are Vampires," I probably would no-vote and move on. This chooses the most generic "insert spooky stuff here" setting imaginable, and doesn't do much with it. Everything feels perfunctory, like it's just going through the list of Vampire Stuff and checking boxes. The lack of a spark, combined with the bad taste in my mouth from the setting, made me fall on the downvote side.

On the other hand, describing vampries as sanguine was pretty funny.

item.content:encoded:
The picture of the underground lake is stunning and I was pretty interested to learn about cooking for vampires, but I didn't enjoy the characterization.

+ show block
– hide block

I kept being pulled out my enjoyment at the beginning by the inconsistent tone of the in-universe author. Sometimes they sound like an ancient vampire:

I have stayed in many hotels in my long unlife, many which have catered exclusively to hemovores like myself.

The venue wants to feed us, and we want to eat! But how to make food that we are actually capable of consuming?

and other times they sound like a cooking YouTube channel.

Every part of the place is specifically designed to be a great experience for all hemovores to relax.

The solution Chaz came up with: just use a lot of blood in the cooking process. If the food is bloody enough, then we'll be able to eat it and keep it down.

I recommend leaning more into the old vampire speech because you mostly stick to that in the latter sections and it works.

Meanwhile hunt section isn't that exciting. It's slow, but because we're seeing it from the vampire's point of view, there's no tension to be heightened by the slower pace. You could introduce some by giving the human a chance to defend themselves, but I think you'd be better off just making the human sacrifice a willing employee of Ambrose's; then you can at least get interesting dialogue about what working under him is like.

The Chaz interview doesn't do anything to flesh out the idea of 'Chaz is a horrible sophisticated monster' more than the rest of the article or even the new Chaz articles do.

We've grown stale as a brand.

I decided I wanted to start pushing the envelope, breaking new ground.

There was plenty of room to expand, innovate and start trying new material. I could finally break free of my shell and start doing what I really wanted to do.

Lots of long hours in the kitchen. Got fairly messy at times.

These are all character traits we learned in Do You Like Huey Lewis and the News. We even already learned that he cooks with blood in that tale! I'd be much more interested to know why Chaz chose to become a vampire, that lifestyle requires dedication and I want to know how he juggles it with being a chef! Him knowing all that would also give the reveal that he's a regular dude way more punch. Right now, the paragraphs about Chaz walking into the light unscathed don't enhance and honestly just slow the reveal down. He doesn't feel enigmatic — he still feels like celebrity chef Hannibal Lecter.

item.content:encoded: I really appreciate the authenticity approach here by Ambrose. The fact that a lot of the experience originates from more conventional approaches than any sort of magical solution (save for the desecration bit) really sells me on the piece. Every detail of the hotel was taken into consideration when crafting this as a haven for vampires, and it really shines in this format.
